A connector is a file that says how to call a web API: where it is, how to sign
in, what each call takes and what it answers. Cascade turns each operation into
a step, with no code to write or run. The format is published (`connector
schema` prints its JSON Schema) and versioned, so a connector written by anyone
runs the same on any Cascade that reads the same version, and the tools to
write, try, publish and install one are in the binary.

A connector can do what an HTTP step can: call one API with one login. What
it adds is that the call is named, its inputs are a form in the editor, the
login is a credential type of its own, and it can be shared as a file.

## Where they live

Connector files are read once, at start, from `HOTLOOP_CASCADE_CONNECTORS_DIR`
(the `connectors` folder inside the data directory by default). A file that
doesn't read is skipped with a warning in the log that says what is wrong with
it, and the rest load. Restart to pick up a change. `hotloop-cascade connector
list` says what is in the folder. Each operation is a step type named
`<connector>.<operation>`, and the connector's credential, if it has one, is a
credential type of its own in the Credentials screen.

Every call goes through the egress policy, so an API on your plant network has
to be allowed (`HOTLOOP_CASCADE_EGRESS_ALLOW`). A connector can only reach the
one base address it names, and a path can't leave it.

## The file

```yaml
connector: 1                 # the spec version; a build refuses one it doesn't read
name: acme-erp               # lowercase letters, digits, dashes; the steps are acme-erp.<operation>
title: Acme ERP
version: 1.2.0
description: Orders and parts from the Acme ERP.
credential:                  # optional: the login the steps use
  title: Acme ERP login
  fields:
    - {name: baseUrl, title: Base URL, required: true}
    - {name: token, title: API token, secret: true, required: true}
base: credential.baseUrl     # an https:// address, or credential.<field>
auth: {type: bearer, field: token}
headers: {X-Client: cascade} # sent on every call
operations:
  - name: getOrder
    title: Get an order
    method: GET              # GET, POST, PUT, PATCH or DELETE
    path: /orders/{id}
    params:
      - {name: id, title: Order id, in: path, required: true}
      - {name: expand, in: query, kind: boolean}
  - name: listOrders
    title: List orders
    method: GET
    path: /orders
    result: {path: data, each: true}
    paginate: {type: cursor, param: cursor, next: meta.next}
  - name: createOrder
    title: Create an order
    method: POST
    path: /orders
    params:
      - {name: customer, in: body, required: true}
      - {name: quantity, in: body, kind: integer}
      - {name: Idempotency-Key, in: header}
```

**auth** is `none`, `bearer` (`field` holds the token), `header` (`name` and
`field`), `query` (`name` and `field`) or `basic` (`username` and `password`
name the credential's fields). Secrets stay in the credential; the file never
holds one.

**params** are an operation's inputs, and become the step's form. `in` says
where one goes: `path` (fills `{name}` in the path, escaped, and has to be
required), `query`, `header`, or `body` (a field of the JSON object sent). `kind` is `string`
(the default), `text`, `number`, `integer`, `boolean`, `object`, `list` or
`options` (with `options: [a, b]`); an object or list goes in the body. A value
that doesn't fit its kind, or a required one that is empty, stops the step
before anything is sent. Like any step input, a param can be an expression.

**result** says where the items are. With no `result` the answer is the
item (a bare value is `{"value": ...}`, text is `{"body": ...}`, an empty
answer is `{"status": 204}`). `path` is a dotted path into the answer, and with
`each: true` the list there becomes one item per element, which is how a step
puts out many items. An answer that is `null` where a list should be is an
empty list.

**paginate** walks a list for you, for a GET with `result.each`. `type: cursor`
sends the cursor in query parameter `param` and reads the next one from the
answer at `next`, and stops when it is empty or missing. `type: page` counts up
from `start` (1) and stops on a page with no items. Either stops at `maxPages`
(100).

A failed call is a failed step with what the API said, sorted the way the
built in connectors sort it: a 429 or a 5xx can be retried by the step's retry
policy, a 4xx can't, and a `Retry-After` is honored. The URL is never put in a
message, because it can carry a key.

## Writing one

```bash
hotloop-cascade connector init acme -o acme.yaml     # a starting point
hotloop-cascade connector validate acme.yaml         # everything wrong with it, in one list
hotloop-cascade connector call acme.yaml getOrder \
    --param id=7 --credential baseUrl=https://erp.plant.lan --credential token=... \
    --allow erp.plant.lan                            # try one operation against the real API
hotloop-cascade connector schema > connector.schema.json   # for your editor
```

`call` runs the operation the way a step would, through the same code, and
prints one JSON line per item.

## Publishing and installing

An index is a static file anyone can host next to the connector files, with
nothing running behind it:

```bash
hotloop-cascade connector index ./published -o ./published/index.yaml
```

`index` reads every connector file in the folder, checks each, and lists
them with a SHA-256 each. Put the folder on any web server. On a Cascade host:

```bash
hotloop-cascade connector install acme --index https://plant.example/connectors/index.yaml
hotloop-cascade connector install acme --index ... --version 1.1.0
```

`install` fetches the index, picks the version (the newest by default), fetches
the file from beside the index, refuses it if its hash isn't the index's or
its name and version aren't the ones asked for, checks it against the spec, and
only then writes it to the connectors directory. Restart Cascade to load it.
Cascade doesn't name an index for you and never fetches one on its own: you
say which, once, and only when you run `install`.
